questions.task: Predict the output

false

questions.correctedCode: Use equals() when the intention is to compare String content.

questions.title: StringBuilder vs String
questions.task: Explain the behavior
questions.answer: String concatenation can create many intermediate String objects, while StringBuilder modifies a mutable character buffer.
questions.explanation: String objects are immutable, so repeated concatenation can create intermediate String objects. StringBuilder is mutable and is generally more suitable for repeated modifications, especially inside loops.
questions.correctedCode: Use StringBuilder when repeatedly building a String in a loop.
followUpQuestions: What happens to intermediate Strings during repeated concatenation?

type-casting.title: Type Casting
type-casting.summary: Practice primitive widening and narrowing, reference upcasting and downcasting, instanceof, polymorphism, ClassCastException, and compile-time versus runtime type rules.
learningGoals: Distinguish primitive casting from reference casting.
Perform downcasting only when the runtime object has the expected subtype.
Understand how reference type affects accessible members while runtime type affects overridden method dispatch.

questions.title: Widening primitive conversion
questions.task: Predict the output and explain why an explicit cast is not required.
questions.expectedBehavior: The integer value is converted to a wider floating-point type without a compilation error.
questions.answer: The output is 100.0.
questions.explanation: Assigning int to double is a widening primitive conversion. Java can perform this conversion implicitly because the destination type has a wider range/representation for this conversion.
hints: Compare the source and destination primitive types.
Is int to double a widening or narrowing conversion?
Does widening normally require an explicit cast?
questions.correctedCode:
int value = 100;
double result = value;
keyTakeaways: Widening conversions can happen implicitly.
int can be assigned to double without an explicit cast.
Widening and narrowing are different conversion categories.
followUpQuestions: Can byte be assigned to int without casting?
Can double be assigned to int without casting?
What happens to precision when converting int to float?

questions.title: Narrowing conversion requires an explicit cast
questions.task: Identify the compilation issue and apply the correct narrowing cast.
questions.expectedBehavior: The code should compile and produce an integer value after an explicit narrowing conversion.
questions.answer: The code does not compile because double to int is a narrowing conversion and requires an explicit cast.
questions.explanation: Narrowing can lose fractional information or range. The explicit cast tells the compiler that the loss is intentional. The fractional part is discarded for this conversion.
hints: Can every double value be represented exactly by int?
Does Java allow this conversion implicitly?
What happens to .99?
keyTakeaways: Narrowing primitive conversions generally require an explicit cast.
Casting double to int discards the fractional part.
Explicit casting does not guarantee that information will be preserved.
followUpQuestions: What happens when the double is larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE?
What is the difference between casting and Math.round()?
Can long be implicitly converted to int?

questions.title: Downcasting to the wrong subtype
questions.task: Predict the runtime exception and explain why the compiler allows the cast.
questions.expectedBehavior: The code compiles but fails at runtime when the actual object is not a Car.
questions.answer: The code compiles but throws ClassCastException because the runtime object is a Bike, not a Car.
questions.explanation: The reference type Vehicle can potentially refer to a Car, so the compiler permits the explicit downcast. At runtime Java checks the actual object type and rejects the cast when it is incompatible.
hints: What is the declared type of v?
What object was actually created?
Which type does the cast require at runtime?
keyTakeaways: Downcasting is checked at runtime.
An incompatible runtime object causes ClassCastException.
instanceof can guard a downcast.
followUpQuestions: Why does the compiler allow the cast?
What is pattern matching for instanceof?
Can a Vehicle reference always be safely cast to Car?

questions.title: Upcasting is implicit and safe
questions.task: Explain why a subclass object can be assigned to a superclass reference without an explicit cast.
questions.expectedBehavior: The assignment compiles and the overridden method uses dynamic dispatch.
questions.answer: The output is Dog.
questions.explanation: Assigning Dog to an Animal reference is upcasting and is implicit. The reference can access members defined by Animal, but overridden instance methods use the runtime object's implementation, so Dog.sound() executes.
hints: Is Dog an Animal?
Does upcasting require an explicit cast?
Which method implementation is selected at runtime?
questions.correctedCode:
Animal animal = new Dog();
animal.sound();
keyTakeaways: Upcasting from subclass to superclass is implicit.
Polymorphic method dispatch uses the runtime object.
The reference type controls which members are accessible at compile time.
followUpQuestions: Can animal.driveDogSpecificMethod() be called directly?
How would downcasting expose a Dog-specific method?
Are fields polymorphic in the same way as methods?

questions.title: Primitive narrowing overflow
questions.task: Predict the result of narrowing a large int to byte and explain the overflow behavior.
questions.expectedBehavior: The result must be explained using the low-order bits retained by the narrowing conversion.
questions.answer: The output is -126.
questions.explanation: byte is an 8-bit signed type. Narrowing from int to byte retains the low-order 8 bits, which represent -126 in signed byte form. The conversion does not throw an exception for this numeric narrowing.
hints: What is the byte range?
Convert 130 to its low-order 8 bits.
Remember that byte is signed.
questions.correctedCode:
int value = 130;
byte result = (byte) value;
keyTakeaways: Narrowing numeric conversion can change the value.
Primitive casts do not throw ClassCastException.
Always consider range loss when narrowing.
followUpQuestions: What is (byte) 128?
What is (byte) 255?
How is primitive casting different from reference casting?

questions.title: instanceof prevents an invalid downcast
questions.task: Correct the code so that process() invokes drive only for Car objects.
questions.expectedBehavior: A Bike should not be cast to Car and should be handled safely.
questions.answer: The direct cast can throw ClassCastException when vehicle is not a Car.
questions.explanation: A Vehicle reference can point to many subclasses. instanceof checks the runtime type before performing the downcast, preventing an invalid cast.
hints: A Vehicle reference does not guarantee a Car object.
Check the runtime type first.
Use pattern matching to combine the check and cast.
keyTakeaways: Use instanceof before unsafe downcasts.
Pattern matching can combine type testing and casting.
Prefer polymorphism when explicit type checks become excessive.
followUpQuestions: When is instanceof a design smell?

What happens if vehicle is null?

questions.title: Reference type controls accessible methods
questions.task: Explain why the compiler rejects the direct call to the subclass-specific method.
questions.expectedBehavior: The code should compile only after a valid downcast.
questions.answer: The code does not compile because fetch() is not declared in Animal.
questions.explanation: The object is a Dog at runtime, but the reference type is Animal. Compile-time member access is based on the reference type. A valid downcast is required to access Dog-specific members.
hints: Look at the declared type of animal.
Is fetch() declared in Animal?
What cast would expose Dog-specific members?
keyTakeaways: Reference type controls compile-time member access.
Runtime type controls overridden method dispatch.
Downcasting exposes subtype-specific members only when valid.
followUpQuestions: Why does animal.sound() work?

questions.title: Casting does not change the object
questions.task: Explain what changes when a reference is cast and what remains unchanged about the actual object.
questions.expectedBehavior: The cast changes the reference's compile-time view, not the runtime object's class.
questions.answer: The output is Bark followed by Dog. Casting does not create a new Dog or change the object's runtime type; it changes how the existing reference is viewed by the compiler.
questions.explanation: animal and dog refer to the same Dog object. The cast enables access to Dog-specific members through the dog reference. The runtime class remains Dog throughout.
hints: How many objects are created?
Do animal and dog point to the same object?
What does a reference cast actually change?
questions.correctedCode:
Animal animal = new Dog();
Dog dog = (Dog) animal; // same object, narrower reference type
keyTakeaways: Casting a reference does not create a new object.
The same object can be viewed through different reference types.
Runtime class remains unchanged after a reference cast.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between casting and object conversion?

equals.title: equals Method
equals.summary: Interview-level practice covering equals contracts, inheritance, null handling, mutable state, and logical equality.

questions.title: equals Without Type Check
questions.task: Identify the problem
questions.answer: The method can throw ClassCastException when obj is not an Employee and NullPointerException when obj is null.
questions.explanation: equals() receives an Object reference. The implementation must check for null and type compatibility before casting the object to Employee.
followUpQuestions: Why does equals() accept Object instead of Employee?
When can ClassCastException occur here?
Why should null be checked before casting?

questions.title: equals and Mutable Fields
questions.task: Identify the equality issue
questions.answer: Changing id changes the logical equality of the object.
questions.explanation: If id defines equality and the value changes while the object is being used in an equality-sensitive collection, the object's logical identity can change unexpectedly.
questions.correctedCode: Use a stable field for logical identity when the object will be used in equality-sensitive collections.
followUpQuestions: Why should equality fields ideally be stable?
How can mutable equality fields cause collection problems?
Why are immutable objects often easier to use as keys?

questions.title: Inheritance and equals
questions.task: Identify the contract issue
questions.answer: Using instanceof in a superclass equals implementation can create equality problems when subclasses add significant state.
questions.explanation: Person can consider an Employee equal based only on name, while Employee may later include employeeId in equality. This can create symmetry or transitivity problems if the subclass changes the equality definition.
questions.correctedCode: Use a consistent equality strategy across the hierarchy, or prefer composition where appropriate.
followUpQuestions: Why can instanceof be problematic in inherited equals implementations?
What is symmetry in equals?
Why is composition sometimes preferred over inheritance for value equality?

questions.title: Objects.equals for Null Safety
questions.task: Predict the output
questions.answer:
false
true
questions.explanation: Objects.equals() safely handles null values. It returns true when both references are null and false when only one reference is null.
questions.correctedCode: No correction is required.
followUpQuestions: What happens if a.equals(b) is called when a is null?
Why is Objects.equals() useful in model classes?

questions.title: Equals Contract: Transitivity
questions.task: Identify the contract being violated
questions.answer: The equals contract violates transitivity.
questions.explanation: The transitivity rule states that if A.equals(B) is true and B.equals(C) is true, then A.equals(C) must also be true.
questions.correctedCode: Design equals() so that equality remains transitive for all valid objects.
followUpQuestions: What are the main properties of the equals contract?
What is the difference between symmetry and transitivity?
How can inheritance accidentally break transitivity?

questions.title: HashSet with Equal Objects
questions.task: Predict the result
questions.explanation: Both Employee objects are equal according to equals() and produce the same hash code. HashSet therefore treats the second object as a duplicate.
questions.correctedCode: No correction is required.
followUpQuestions: Why must equal objects have equal hash codes?

questions.title: HashMap with Inconsistent hashCode
questions.task: Predict the lookup result
questions.answer: null
questions.explanation: k1 and k2 are equal according to equals(), but their hash codes can differ because identityHashCode() is based on object identity. HashMap uses the hash to locate the appropriate bucket, so it may not find the entry stored using k1.
questions.correctedCode: Return a hash based on the same logical field used by equals(), such as Integer.hashCode(id).
followUpQuestions: What is the hashCode contract for equal objects?
Why does HashMap use hashCode() before equals()?
How can a broken hashCode() implementation cause lookup failures?

questions.title: Mutable HashMap Key
questions.task: Explain the lookup problem
questions.answer: null
questions.explanation: The key was inserted using the hash code for id 1. After id changes to 2, the key produces a different hash code, so HashMap searches using a different bucket and cannot locate the existing entry.
questions.correctedCode: Do not modify fields used by equals() and hashCode() while the object is being used as a HashMap key.
followUpQuestions: Why are immutable keys preferred?
What changes when key.id is modified?
Can the entry still physically exist inside the HashMap?

questions.title: Hash Collision Does Not Mean Equality
questions.task: Evaluate the statement
questions.answer: p1 and p2 can have the same hash code without being equal.
questions.explanation: The hashCode contract allows unequal objects to have the same hash code. This situation is called a hash collision.
questions.correctedCode: No correction is required, although a good hash function should generally provide a good distribution of hash values.
followUpQuestions: Why are hash collisions allowed?
How does HashMap handle collisions?
Does hashCode() uniquely identify an object?

questions.title: HashCode Fields Must Match equals
questions.task: Identify the bug
questions.answer: hashCode() uses name even though equals() only uses id.
questions.explanation: Two User objects with the same id but different names are equal according to equals(), but they can produce different hash codes. This violates the equals-hashCode contract.
questions.correctedCode: return Integer.hashCode(id);
followUpQuestions: Why must hashCode() use fields consistent with equals()?
What can happen in HashSet if this bug exists?

compare.title: compareTo and Comparator
compare.summary: Interview-level practice covering Comparable, Comparator, sorting contracts, null handling, and multi-field ordering.

questions.title: compareTo Using Subtraction
questions.task: Identify the problem
questions.answer: Subtraction can overflow and produce an incorrect comparison result for extreme integer values.
questions.explanation: Using Integer.compare() avoids integer overflow and clearly expresses the intended comparison.
questions.correctedCode: return Integer.compare(this.age, other.age);
followUpQuestions: Why can subtraction overflow in compareTo()?
Why is Integer.compare() safer?
What does compareTo() return when two values are equal?

questions.title: Comparable vs Comparator
questions.task: Choose the appropriate approach
questions.answer: Use Comparable for the natural ordering and Comparator for alternate orderings such as sorting by name.
questions.explanation: Comparable defines one natural ordering inside the class. Comparator allows multiple external sorting strategies without changing the class's natural ordering.
questions.correctedCode: Comparator<Employee> byName = Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName);
followUpQuestions: When should Comparable be used?
Why can multiple Comparators be useful?
Can a class have multiple natural orderings?

questions.title: Comparator Returning Zero
questions.task: Predict the effect
questions.answer: The comparator treats all elements as equal for ordering purposes, so no meaningful sorting is performed.
questions.explanation: A comparator returning zero means the two elements are considered equivalent according to that ordering.
questions.correctedCode: names.sort(String::compareTo);
followUpQuestions: What does returning zero from compare() mean?
Can two different objects compare as zero?
How can an inconsistent comparator affect sorted collections?

questions.title: Comparator with thenComparing
questions.task: Predict the sorting rule
questions.answer: Employees are sorted by name first and by age when their names are equal.
questions.explanation: thenComparingInt() adds a secondary ordering. The age comparison is used only when the primary name comparison considers two employees equal.
questions.correctedCode: No correction is required.
followUpQuestions: What happens when two employees have different names?
Why is a secondary comparator useful?
How can the age ordering be reversed?

questions.title: compareTo Consistency with equals
questions.task: Identify the collection issue
questions.answer: compareTo() can return 0 for employees with the same id but different names even though equals() returns false.
questions.explanation: Natural ordering is inconsistent with equals because compareTo() considers only id while equals() considers both id and name. This can cause surprising behavior in TreeSet and TreeMap.
questions.correctedCode: Make compareTo() consistent with equals when possible, for example by comparing id and then name.
followUpQuestions: Why can TreeSet behave differently from HashSet here?
Does compareTo() returning 0 always mean equals() must return true?
Why is consistency between compareTo() and equals() recommended?

questions.expectedBehavior: Every update to the static invariant uses one common lock or atomic variable.
questions.answer: Each synchronized run locks its own Worker instance, so the threads hold different monitors while racing on the shared static count.
questions.explanation:
The lock must match state ownership. Static state is shared across every instance; use a static synchronized method/class lock, a dedicated static lock, or AtomicInteger. Synchronization on different objects supplies no mutual exclusion or happens-before between the updates.

Prefer avoiding global mutable state. If count is a metric under high contention, LongAdder may fit; if exact transition semantics matter, AtomicInteger or locking is clearer.

questions.title: Availability check is outside the synchronized block
questions.task: Two threads can both pass the ticket check and then decrement below zero. Move the atomic boundary to protect the full check-and-update invariant and return an honest result.

Mutual exclusion must cover the whole check-then-act sequence. Enter the lock before reading the guarded state, re-evaluate the condition, update, and decide the return while still inside. Locking only the write does not make the earlier decision valid.

AtomicInteger.update/CAS could implement this single-field transition, but a synchronized method is simpler and extends naturally if reservations later update related fields.

keyTakeaways: The values() iteration is not protected for its full duration.

Why: synchronizedMap synchronizes individual method calls, but its collection views require manual synchronization during traversal.
Fix: Wrap the complete loop in synchronized (scores), or take an appropriately protected snapshot.

questions.title: ConcurrentHashMap containsKey-then-put still races
questions.task: Two threads initialize an expensive service for one key. The map is thread-safe, yet factory executes twice and one created service leaks. Make installation atomic and discuss mapping-function constraints.
questions.expectedBehavior: Install exactly one mapping and dispose/avoid unnecessary duplicate creation according to factory semantics.
questions.answer: containsKey and put are individually safe but not one atomic check-then-act operation. Multiple threads can construct services and overwrite/lose one result.
questions.explanation:
Use computeIfAbsent for per-key atomic initialization when the mapping function is short and does not recursively mutate the same map/key. It can be invoked under internal coordination; avoid slow blocking work when possible. If construction has external side effects or resources, a Future/holder initialization design may better control one-time creation and failure.

putIfAbsent avoids overwrite but can still construct multiple candidate values before the call.
hints: Can another thread act between two map calls?
Which method combines absence test and mapping?
Does putIfAbsent avoid pre-call construction?
keyTakeaways: Thread-safe methods do not make multi-call sequences atomic.
computeIfAbsent expresses atomic per-key initialization.
Mapping functions should avoid slow/recursive side effects.
followUpQuestions: What happens when the mapping function returns null?
How are exceptions from the mapping function handled?
How would you cache failed initialization?

questions.title: Concurrent frequency update loses increments
questions.task: The ConcurrentHashMap contains Integer counters, but get-or-default plus put loses updates. Replace it with an atomic per-key operation and then discuss LongAdder for high contention.
questions.expectedBehavior: Every increment is retained for each word.
questions.answer: The read-modify-write spans two map operations. Two threads can read the same current value and both store the same incremented value.
questions.explanation:
Use map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum), whose per-key remapping is atomic under ConcurrentHashMap's contract. For very hot metric counters, use ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> and computeIfAbsent(...).increment(), a pattern documented by the API.

LongAdder.sum is not an atomic global decision snapshot, so use it for statistics rather than inventory/one-time transitions.
hints: Which steps can interleave?
Which Map method combines insert and aggregation?
What type spreads contended counter updates?

merge performs an atomic per-key update.
LongAdder improves contended statistics but not transactional decisions.

How would an exact cross-key total be obtained?

Avoid global-invariant assumptions across independent atomic keys.

multithreading.title: Java Memory Model & happens-before
multithreading.summary: Prove visibility using monitor, volatile, start, join, final-field, and concurrent-handoff edges. Reject sleep/timing, mixed locks, constructor escape, and final-reference misconceptions.
learningGoals: Separate visibility, ordering, atomicity, and exclusion.
Find data races even when tests pass.

questions.title: Writer and reader synchronize on different locks
questions.task: Explain why both methods being synchronized blocks does not publish data and ready correctly. Use one happens-before path.
questions.expectedBehavior: If reader observes ready, it must observe data=42.
questions.answer: Unlocking writeLock has no happens-before relation to later locking readLock. The accesses still race.
questions.explanation: Monitor visibility requires the same monitor. Use one lock for both, or publish with a volatile ready flag written after data and read before data. Different locks provide independent ordering domains.
hints: Which monitor edge does JLS define?
keyTakeaways: Same-monitor unlock/lock creates happens-before.
Different locks do not coordinate.
Both readers and writers follow one protocol.
followUpQuestions: How would volatile ready publish data?
Would volatile data alone protect the pair?

questions.title: Volatile flag is written before the data
questions.task: The reader can observe ready=true and stale data. Reverse the publication order and prove the happens-before chain.
questions.expectedBehavior: A reader that sees ready=true sees data=42.
questions.answer: The volatile write occurs before data=42, so it cannot publish a later ordinary write to a reader after the volatile read.
questions.explanation: Program order must be data=42 then volatile ready=true. The volatile write happens-before a subsequent read that observes it; transitivity carries the preceding data write to the reader's later data read.
hints: Which ordinary writes occur before the volatile write?
questions.correctedCode: void write(){ data=42; ready=true; }
keyTakeaways: Publication order matters.
Volatile write publishes preceding actions.
Reader checks volatile before dependent fields.
followUpQuestions: What if writer resets ready?
How would an immutable snapshot simplify this?

questions.title: Thread.start safely publishes pre-start configuration
questions.task: Determine whether volatile is required for input written before start and output read after join. State both lifecycle happens-before rules.
questions.expectedBehavior: Print 42 with no data race under the shown ordering.
questions.answer: The code correctly prints 42. Pre-start actions happen-before worker actions, and worker actions happen-before successful join return.
questions.explanation: input does not need volatile because start publishes earlier configuration. output does not need volatile because join publishes worker completion. Mutating input after start or reading output before join would require separate coordination.
hints: Which APIs create lifecycle synchronization edges?
questions.correctedCode: // No correction required for this exact ordering.
keyTakeaways: start publishes prior actions to the child.
join publishes child actions to the joiner.
Use lifecycle edges instead of redundant volatile fields.
followUpQuestions: What if worker starts before input assignment?
What if join times out?

questions.title: this escapes from constructor
questions.task: The constructor starts a thread before all fields are assigned. Explain how the callback can observe partial state and refactor construction/publication.
questions.expectedBehavior: No other thread obtains this until construction finishes.
questions.answer: The code also fails definite assignment for final id usage before assignment; more generally, starting a thread from a constructor exposes this before construction and can observe partial/default state.
questions.explanation: Complete all final/nonfinal initialization, return the object, then let an owner start/register it. Final-field guarantees assume proper construction without escape. Avoid overridable callbacks/listener registration/thread start inside constructors.
hints: When does the new thread receive this?
Has the constructor completed?
keyTakeaways: Do not publish this during construction.
Complete immutable state before start/registration.
Final fields have special safe-construction semantics.
followUpQuestions: Can a constructor call an overridable method safely?
How do factories help?

questions.title: final List reference is still mutable shared state
questions.task: Explain why final does not make concurrent add/iteration safe and publish an immutable value instead.
questions.expectedBehavior: Readers see a stable immutable list without concurrent mutation.
questions.answer: final prevents reassigning names but does not synchronize or freeze ArrayList contents. Concurrent add/iteration is a data race and can fail.
questions.explanation: Use a lock for mutation/traversal, a concurrent structure with fitting semantics, or replace immutable snapshots through volatile/AtomicReference. Ownership and mutability are distinct from reference reassignment.
hints: What operation does final prohibit?
keyTakeaways: final reference is not deep immutability.
ArrayList remains non-thread-safe.
Immutable snapshot replacement enables lock-free reads.
followUpQuestions: Why is names volatile in the snapshot version?
When would CopyOnWriteArrayList fit?

questions.title: Thread.onSpinWait does not create visibility
questions.task: The loop calls onSpinWait and assumes it refreshes done. Explain the data race and add a proper synchronization mechanism.
questions.expectedBehavior: Worker termination is observed portably.
questions.answer: onSpinWait is a processor/runtime hint for spin loops, not a memory synchronization action. done remains a racy ordinary field and the loop may not terminate.
questions.explanation: Use volatile/AtomicBoolean for a spin flag, or better join/latch when waiting for completion. Spinning consumes CPU and should be reserved for measured low-latency designs.
hints: Does onSpinWait appear in JMM synchronizes-with rules?
keyTakeaways: CPU hints do not create happens-before.
Use join for completion.
Avoid wasteful spins without measured need.

multithreading.title: Locks, Conditions & Atomics
multithreading.summary: Debug explicit-lock cleanup, Condition ownership/guard loops, read/write effects, CAS retries, side-effectful update functions, ABA/versioning, and LongAdder limitations.

questions.title: Exception leaks ReentrantLock
questions.task: Explain why later callers block forever when update throws and apply the canonical pattern.
questions.expectedBehavior: Release the lock on normal and abrupt completion.
questions.answer: risky throws before unlock, leaving the lock owned. Subsequent threads block.
questions.explanation: Place unlock in finally immediately after successful lock acquisition. ReentrantLock does not have structured automatic release like synchronized.
hints: Which statement is skipped after throw?
keyTakeaways: Explicit locks require explicit finally cleanup.
Acquire then immediately enter try.
Exceptions must not leak ownership.
followUpQuestions: How does tryLock change the pattern?
Why might synchronized be safer here?

questions.title: Condition await called without lock
questions.task: Predict the failure and implement the guarded-wait pattern.
questions.expectedBehavior: Wait while empty, then remove after signal under the same lock.
questions.answer: await throws IllegalMonitorStateException because the current thread does not hold the associated lock.
questions.explanation: Acquire lock, test predicate in while, await (which releases/reacquires the lock), update state, and unlock in finally. Signallers also hold the lock and change state before signal.
hints: What ownership does Condition require?
Why while rather than if?
keyTakeaways: Condition is bound to one Lock.
await in a while predicate loop.
unlock in finally.
followUpQuestions: When use signalAll?
How does await compare with Object.wait?

questions.title: Atomic update function sends duplicate emails
questions.task: updateAndGet may invoke its function more than once under CAS contention. Explain why the side effect can repeat and separate atomic state calculation from effects.
questions.expectedBehavior: State transition is atomic and email is emitted once only after this call wins the transition.
questions.answer: CAS update functions may be retried if another thread changes state. sendEmail can run multiple times even though one value is installed.
questions.explanation: Keep update functions pure. For a one-way transition, compareAndSet NEW->RUNNING and send only when it returns true. Even then, a crash between state and email may require an outbox/idempotency design for exactly-once business effects.
hints: Can updateAndGet retry its function?
Which boolean operation reports the winning transition?
keyTakeaways: CAS functions may retry.
Keep atomic update functions side-effect-free.
External exactly-once effects need stronger protocols.
followUpQuestions: What is ABA?
How would an outbox help?

questions.title: Two AtomicIntegers do not preserve one invariant
questions.task: A transfer decrements available then increments reserved. Readers can observe an invalid total. Preserve the pair as one atomic state transition.
questions.expectedBehavior: available + reserved always equals capacity for every observed version.
questions.answer: Each variable update is atomic, but the pair is not. A reader can run between operations and observe total 9.
questions.explanation: Use one lock guarding both fields or one AtomicReference to an immutable record and update the whole pair with one CAS. Independent atomics do not create a multi-variable transaction.
hints: How many linearization points exist?
keyTakeaways: Atomic variables protect individual values.
Cross-field invariants need one atomic boundary.
Immutable aggregate CAS is one option.
followUpQuestions: When is a lock simpler?
Can the update function have side effects?

questions.title: LongAdder sum is used as a hard limit
questions.task: Multiple threads use LongAdder.sum before increment to enforce max 10 active jobs. Explain why more than 10 can start and choose an exact primitive.
questions.expectedBehavior: Check-and-increment the hard limit atomically.
questions.answer: sum and increment are separate, and LongAdder sum is not an atomic snapshot under concurrent updates. Many threads can pass before increments become visible in the sum.
questions.explanation: LongAdder is for scalable statistics, not hard limits. Use a Semaphore(10), or an AtomicInteger CAS loop/lock that combines check and increment. Semaphore directly models permits and supports release/fairness/timed acquisition.
hints: Is sum+increment one operation?
Which concurrent primitive models 10 permits?
keyTakeaways: LongAdder favors throughput statistics.
Its sum is not a hard-limit transaction.
Semaphore models bounded concurrent permits.
followUpQuestions: What if exit releases twice?
When use AtomicInteger instead?

questions.title: Read lock attempts unsafe upgrade
questions.task: A method holds ReentrantReadWriteLock.readLock and calls writeLock.lock when cache is missing. Explain the deadlock/upgrade hazard and use release-then-acquire with recheck.
questions.expectedBehavior: No thread waits for a write lock while retaining a read hold that prevents that write lock.
questions.answer: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not safely support upgrading a held read lock to write. The thread can wait for all readers—including its own read hold—to release.
questions.explanation: Release the read lock, acquire write, recheck because another writer may have initialized, update, then optionally downgrade by acquiring read before releasing write. Simpler synchronized/volatile initialization may be preferable.
hints: Can write lock be granted while any read hold remains?
Why recheck after acquiring write?
keyTakeaways: Read-to-write upgrade is hazardous.
Release, acquire write, and recheck.
Use simpler synchronization unless read/write benefits are measured.
followUpQuestions: How does lock downgrading work?
Would volatile double-check be simpler?

multithreading.title: Executors, Futures & CompletableFuture
multithreading.summary: Debug pool admission, unbounded queues, starvation, ignored Future failures, timeout/cancel semantics, CompletableFuture executor selection/composition, periodic-task failure, and two-phase shutdown.
learningGoals: Own and shut down executors correctly.

questions.title: Unbounded queue makes maximumPoolSize ineffective
questions.task: A ThreadPoolExecutor has core=2, max=20, but only two workers process a huge backlog. Explain admission behavior and configure bounded overload policy.
questions.expectedBehavior: Queue capacity and rejection reflect downstream throughput instead of unbounded latency/memory.
questions.answer: The unbounded queue accepts tasks after core threads are busy, so the executor normally never creates workers beyond core and max=20 has no practical effect.
questions.explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor admission is core workers -> queue -> extra up to max if queue is full -> rejection. Use a deliberate bounded queue and rejection policy after measuring CPU/I/O/downstream capacity. More threads are not free and can overload dependencies.
hints: When are threads beyond core created?
Can this queue become full in practice?
keyTakeaways: Unbounded queue hides overload.
max threads activate only after queue rejection/fullness.
Capacity/rejection are reliability decisions.
followUpQuestions: How does CallerRuns create backpressure?
How would CPU-bound sizing differ?

questions.title: Fixed pool starves on child Future.get
questions.task: Two parent tasks occupy both workers, submit child tasks to the same pool, and block on get. Explain task-dependency starvation and refactor with non-blocking composition or separate ownership.
questions.expectedBehavior: Child work can execute without requiring a worker held by its waiting parent.
questions.answer: Both workers run parents and wait for children queued to the same pool. No worker remains to run children, so progress stops.
questions.explanation: This is thread-pool starvation/dependency deadlock, not a monitor cycle. Avoid blocking inside tasks for same-pool children. Compose CompletableFutures, compute child inline, use a work-stealing design appropriate to tasks, or separate executors with bounded capacity based on dependency domains.
hints: How many workers are free after parents start?
Where are child tasks?
keyTakeaways: Blocking child dependencies can starve a fixed pool.
Use non-blocking stage composition.
Diagnose task dependency, not only lock cycles.
followUpQuestions: Can CompletableFuture still starve if a stage calls join?
When use separate executors?

questions.title: Future timeout leaves work running
questions.task: Caller times out and assumes the task stopped. Explain the lifecycle and explicitly decide cancellation.
questions.expectedBehavior: After timeout, request interruption when appropriate and handle non-cooperative work honestly.
questions.answer: Timed get only stops the caller from waiting; the task may continue using resources and later complete.
questions.explanation: Call cancel(true) if interruption is an appropriate cooperative cancellation request, and design slowCall to honor it/API-specific timeouts. cancel does not roll back completed side effects or forcibly stop non-interruptible operations.
hints: What method changes Future cancellation state?
keyTakeaways: Timeout and cancellation differ.
cancel(true) is a request.
Underlying APIs need their own deadlines/cancellation.
followUpQuestions: What does get throw after successful cancellation?
Can CompletableFuture orTimeout interrupt its supplier?

questions.title: thenApply creates nested CompletableFuture
questions.task: A function already returns CompletableFuture<Order>. Explain why thenApply produces CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> and flatten it.
questions.expectedBehavior: One CompletableFuture<Order> that completes when the async order lookup completes.
questions.answer: thenApply maps T to U exactly; here U itself is CompletableFuture<Order>. Use thenCompose to flatten dependent asynchronous stages.
questions.explanation: thenCompose is the async analogue of flatMap. thenCombine is for independent stages whose results are combined. Executor choice matters: Async variants without explicit executor use the common pool.
hints: Does the callback return a plain Order or a future?
questions.correctedCode: CompletableFuture<Order> order=user.thenCompose(u -> loadOrder(u.id()));
keyTakeaways: thenApply transforms values.
thenCompose flattens dependent async work.
thenCombine joins independent stages.
followUpQuestions: Where does a non-Async continuation run?
How would failures be recovered?

questions.title: Periodic task silently stops after one exception
questions.task: A scheduled heartbeat runs twice and then never again after a RuntimeException. Explain ScheduledExecutorService periodic semantics and keep expected failures observable while continuing.
questions.expectedBehavior: Each scheduled run handles expected failure and the periodic series continues according to policy.
questions.buggyCode:
ScheduledExecutorService s=Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
s.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> sendHeartbeat(),0,1,SECONDS);
questions.answer: If a periodic execution throws and the exception escapes, subsequent executions are suppressed.
questions.explanation: Catch expected operational exceptions inside the Runnable, record/metric them, and decide whether continuing is safe. Do not catch fatal programming/invariant problems merely to keep a corrupt loop alive. Retain ScheduledFuture for cancellation/status and shut down the scheduler owner.
hints: What does the periodic scheduling contract say after exceptional execution?
keyTakeaways: Escaping failure stops future periodic executions.
Handle expected failures inside task.
Retain lifecycle ownership and observability.
followUpQuestions: Fixed rate versus fixed delay?
Can one execution overlap itself?

questions.title: shutdownNow is treated as guaranteed termination
questions.task: The application calls shutdownNow and immediately closes shared files while tasks may still run. Implement two-phase shutdown and explain cooperation.
questions.expectedBehavior: Stop submissions, wait, request interruption, wait again, and close shared resources only after termination/explicit failure policy.
questions.buggyCode:
pool.shutdownNow();
sharedFile.close();
questions.answer: shutdownNow only attempts to interrupt active tasks and returns queued never-started tasks. It does not wait or guarantee that tasks terminate.
questions.explanation: Use shutdown, awaitTermination, then shutdownNow if the deadline expires, then await again. Preserve caller interruption and handle queued returned tasks. Tasks must honor interruption; non-interruptible code can outlive the request.
hints: Which method waits for termination?
What does shutdownNow return?
keyTakeaways: shutdownNow is best effort and non-waiting.
Use two-phase owner shutdown.
Tasks must cooperate with interruption.

multithreading.title: Interruption, Cancellation & Shutdown
multithreading.summary: Debug interrupt-status clearing, propagation/restoration, CPU-loop cancellation points, Future.cancel, timeout versus cancellation, resource/invariant cleanup, and executor ownership.

questions.title: Thread.interrupted clears the signal in a loop condition
questions.task: The loop calls Thread.interrupted twice per iteration and misses a signal during cleanup logic. Explain clearing behavior and use a non-clearing check.
questions.expectedBehavior: Once interruption is requested, the loop exits and status remains available to outer code if policy requires.
questions.answer: Thread.interrupted checks the current thread and clears status. The first or second check can consume the signal, making later checks false.
questions.explanation: Use isInterrupted for non-clearing observation. Use Thread.interrupted only when intentionally consuming the signal. A single owner should define whether status is restored before return.
hints: Which check has a clearing side effect?
questions.correctedCode: while(!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()){ doWork(); }

isInterrupted does not clear.
Cancellation policy owns consumption/restoration.

questions.expectedBehavior: Task exits promptly after interrupt without corrupting shared output.
questions.answer: The loop never blocks or checks interrupt status, so interruption request does not force it to stop.

hints: Where is an interruption check or interruptible call?
keyTakeaways: Interrupt cannot forcibly stop CPU code.
Add cooperative cancellation points.
Preserve state invariants on exit.

questions.title: InterruptedException is wrapped without restoring status
questions.task: A Runnable adapter wraps InterruptedException in a domain exception. Preserve both cancellation status and cause.
questions.expectedBehavior: Outer executor/lifecycle code can observe interruption, and diagnostics retain the original exception.

try{queue.take();}
catch(InterruptedException e){throw new WorkerException("failed");}

Preserve causes during translation.
Normal shutdown may not be an error.

questions.task: Caller returns “not charged” after timeout while background payment may complete. Explain unknown outcome and design idempotent/cancellable operation semantics.
questions.expectedBehavior: Never claim failure/success without reconciling operation state; retries are deduplicated.
questions.answer: The timeout only stops waiting; charge may complete afterward. Returning notCharged can be false and a retry can double-charge.
questions.explanation: Use gateway deadline/cancellation if supported, idempotency key, and an UNKNOWN/PENDING outcome reconciled by status lookup. cancel(true) may not interrupt network/library code and never reverses a completed charge.

Cancellation is best effort.
Side effects need idempotency/reconciliation.

questions.title: Cancellation leaves lock-protected state half transitioned
questions.task: An interruptible call occurs between decrement and increment of one invariant. Ensure cancellation restores/commits atomically before releasing the lock.
questions.expectedBehavior: Invariant available+reserved remains constant even if interrupted.

Keep blocking external calls outside locks.
Cancellation-safe design preserves invariants.

questions.title: Library shuts down an executor it borrowed
questions.task: A helper receives a shared ExecutorService, submits one task, and shuts it down. Explain why unrelated application tasks are later rejected and fix lifecycle ownership.

questions.task: Explain how a notification can be missed when the state is updated after notify, then fix the ordering.

Singleton Design Pattern.title: Singleton Design Pattern
Singleton Design Pattern.summary: Interview-level debugging practice covering lazy initialization, multithreading, double-checked locking, reflection, serialization, cloning, classloaders, and enum singletons.

questions.title: Classic Lazy Singleton Race Condition
questions.task: Identify the bug and predict behavior under concurrency
questions.answer: Multiple threads calling getInstance() concurrently when instance is null can create multiple instances, violating the singleton property.
questions.explanation: The check `if (instance == null)` is not synchronized. If two threads evaluate the condition simultaneously before either assigns `instance`, both will execute `new LazySingleton()`, creating distinct objects.
followUpQuestions: Why is synchronizing the entire method considered a performance bottleneck?

questions.title: Broken Double-Checked Locking (Missing Volatile)
questions.task: Identify the subtle multithreading bug
questions.answer: Instruction reordering during object instantiation can allow another thread to observe a non-null, partially constructed instance.
questions.explanation: Object creation (`new DclSingleton()`) involves memory allocation, constructor execution, and reference assignment. Without the `volatile` modifier, compiler and CPU instruction reordering can assign the memory reference to `instance` before the constructor finishes, exposing a partially initialized object to other threads.
questions.correctedCode: private static volatile DclSingleton instance;
followUpQuestions: How does the `volatile` keyword prevent instruction reordering?

questions.title: Breaking Singleton via Reflection
questions.task: Explain how the pattern is broken and fix it
questions.answer: Reflection can bypass `private` access modifiers using `setAccessible(true)` and invoke the constructor to create a second instance.
questions.explanation: Java reflection can inspect and invoke private constructors. To prevent this, the constructor should check if an instance already exists and throw an exception if an attempt is made to construct another one.

questions.title: Breaking Singleton via Object Cloning
questions.task: Identify why multiple instances are created
questions.answer: Calling `clone()` on `CloneableSingleton` creates a separate shallow copy of the object.
questions.explanation: Because the singleton inherits `Cloneable` from its superclass, callers can invoke `clone()` to create a duplicate object in the heap without going through `getInstance()`.

questions.title: Bill Pugh Singleton (Initialization-on-Demand Holder)
questions.task: Explain when the instance is loaded and why it is thread-safe
questions.answer: The instance is initialized lazily only when `getInstance()` is called, and JVM class loading mechanics guarantee thread safety without explicit synchronization.
questions.explanation: The nested static class `SingletonHelper` is not loaded into memory when `BillPughSingleton` is loaded. It only loads when `SingletonHelper.INSTANCE` is referenced. The JVM handles class initialization with internal locks, providing thread safety and lazy loading with zero synchronization overhead.
questions.correctedCode: The code is correct as designed and serves as a best-practice static holder pattern.

questions.title: State Mutation in Enum Singleton
questions.task: Identify the thread-safety flaw with mutable state
questions.answer: The enum provides a singleton instance, but the instance method `increment()` and field `counter` are not thread-safe.
questions.explanation: Enums inherently protect against reflection, serialization, and multi-threaded instance creation. However, standard object state rules still apply: mutable fields inside an Enum singleton require synchronization or atomic wrappers to be safe under concurrent access.

questions.title: Classloader Scope Issue
questions.task: Explain how multiple instances can exist in a single JVM
questions.answer: If the singleton class is loaded by two different ClassLoaders, each ClassLoader will maintain its own distinct `INSTANCE`.
questions.explanation: In Java, static fields are scoped per `java.lang.Class` object per `ClassLoader`. In environments with multiple class loaders (such as OSGi or enterprise application servers), two different classloaders can load the class independently, creating multiple singleton instances.
questions.correctedCode: Ensure the Singleton class is loaded by a shared parent ClassLoader (such as System/Application ClassLoader) or manage instances via dependency injection containers.

questions.title: Eager Initialization with Unhandled Exception in Static Block
questions.task: Predict the behavior if initialization throws an exception
questions.answer: If the constructor throws an unhandled exception, the JVM throws `java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError`, and subsequent calls to `getInstance()` fail with `java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError`.
questions.explanation: Static initializer failure causes class initialization to fail permanently. The class remains in an erroneous state, preventing any further interactions or recovery during runtime.

questions.title: Subclassing and Factory Misconfiguration
questions.task: Identify why singleton integrity is broken
questions.answer: Protected constructors and non-final classes allow subclasses to instantiate new objects, breaking the single-instance constraint.
questions.explanation: Using `protected` constructors allows any subclass or package-level class to invoke `new ExtendedConfigManager()`, creating additional instances. Singletons should have `private` constructors and typically be marked `final` to prohibit subclassing.
